extracted.intended_audience: educational psychologists, SRL researchers, instructional designers, and teachers interested in self-regulated learning theory and interventions
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative review of major self-regulated learning (SRL) models, identifying their emphases (cognition, motivation, emotion), conceptual distinctions (e.g., TD/BU, automaticity, context), empirical support from meta-analyses, and implications for intervention and measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognition (model emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which a given SRL model emphasizes cognitive processes (metacognition, task analysis, monitoring, strategy use) as central to self-regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review classifies models by relative emphasis on cognition (Table 3). Efklides, Winne, and SSRL/Pintrich are variously positioned across levels; models differ on whether cognition is foregrounded (e.g., Efklides, Winne) vs. secondary. Consider how models represent cognitive subprocesses (monitoring, explicitness, task×person interactions) when choosing or evaluating a model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation (model emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which a model conceptualizes motivation and motivational beliefs (self-efficacy, goal orientation, effort regulation) as central SRL components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some models (Zimmerman, Boekaerts, Pintrich) place strong emphasis on motivational beliefs across phases (forethought includes self-motivation beliefs). SSRL and others include motivation but may not differentiate components in detail. Meta-analytic findings highlight goal level, persistence, effort, and self-efficacy as strong predictors of learning; interventions including motivational strategies show larger effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion (model emphasis and emotion-regulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how a model incorporates affective processes and emotion-regulation strategies into SRL (e.g., emotions influencing goal pathways, affective reactions during self-evaluation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boekaerts strongly emphasizes emotions influencing goal pathways (learning vs. well-being); Pintrich and Zimmerman emphasize affective reactions during self-evaluation and mention strategies to monitor and manage emotions. SSRL and Efklides/Winne acknowledge affect but may not specify emotion-regulation subprocesses. Negative automatic emotions can undermine learning, so awareness and regulation strategies are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top–Down / Bottom–Up (TD/BU) orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a model frames regulation as top–down (goals/person-guided), bottom–up (data/task-driven), or interactionist (reciprocal cycles between cognition, behavior, environment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boekaerts' mastery (top–down) vs. well-being (bottom–up) pathways; Efklides defines top–down as person-characteristic-guided and bottom–up as data-driven. Zimmerman and Winne argue for interactionist/recursive cycles rather than strict TD/BU. Use this criterion to judge whether a model suits contexts where goal-setting vs. task-driven monitoring is primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automaticity / implicit processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Role attributed to automatic or implicit (non-conscious) processes in SRL, including automatization of strategies and implicit activation of goals or cognitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Winne and Efklides describe much cognition as implicit; Zimmerman discusses automization of strategies (strategy use can become automatic and executed with less metacognitive monitoring). Automatic processes can reduce cognitive load and enable strategy use, but some automatic emotions or reactions may be detrimental; interventions should help learners trace cognitive products (notes, underlines) and bring problematic automatic processes to awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and social influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion and treatment of environmental/contextual factors (task context, classroom climate, group members, teachers) and their role in promoting or constraining SRL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All models include context to some degree, but SSRL emphasizes context and social sources as promoters of individual or joint regulation; Zimmerman's triadic/multi-level models foreground vicarious learning and context in skill development. Consider context when designing interventions (environmental structuring, social scaffolding) and note limited empirical work on diverse contexts outside SSRL authors' work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phases of SRL (forethought, performance, self-reflection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how a model divides SRL into temporal phases—forethought (planning, motivation), performance (monitoring, volition), and self-reflection (self-evaluation, reactions influencing future tasks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zimmerman's cyclical model explicitly uses forethought, performance/volitional control, and self-reflection; forethought includes self-motivation beliefs, performance emphasizes volition and monitoring, and self-reflection affects future motivation and task choices. Use phases to structure instruction and assessment of SRL processes across time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative / socially-shared regulation (SSRL)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the model accounts for group-level regulation processes—how groups jointly regulate learning and how social interaction affects individual SRL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SSRL (Hadwin et al.) explicitly includes group-regulation processes and motivation in collaborative settings; authors note significant emotional challenges in collaborative learning and empirical studies on group-level motivation regulation. SSRL-based interventions require careful implementation (differential effects by educational level) and may need scaffolding to support joint regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative emphasis levels across models (levels of relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comparative classification that ranks models by first/second/third level emphasis on cognition, motivation, and emotion (as presented in Table 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review proposes reading these levels as a continuum. Use this classification to quickly identify which models foreground which SRL areas (e.g., Winne and Efklides often emphasize cognition; Boekaerts emphasizes emotion and motivational pathways). This helps select models aligned with research or intervention priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/design criteria for effective SRL interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-analytic and review-based findings about what features make SRL interventions more effective (contextualization, domain-specific tasks, learner activity, metacognitive awareness, inclusion of motivational strategies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hattie et al. recommend training: (a) be in context, (b) use tasks within the same domain as the target content, and (c) promote a high degree of learner activity and metacognitive awareness. Dignath et al. found greater effect sizes when interventions included metacognitive and motivational strategies and when theoretical background matched educational level (socio-cognitive for primary; metacognitive for secondary). Apply these design criteria when developing SRL interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key predictors to target (goal level, persistence, effort, self-efficacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical identification of the strongest SRL-related predictors of learning outcomes to prioritize in interventions and measurement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sitzmann & Ely report that goal level, persistence, effort, and self-efficacy had the strongest effects and together accounted for 17% of variance in learning beyond ability and prior knowledge. Richardson et al. and Robbins et al. also highlight self-efficacy and achievement motivation as top predictors. Interventions should explicitly target these constructs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental tailoring of SRL interventions by educational level
rubrics_metrics.description: Guideline that different SRL models and intervention emphases work better at different educational stages (primary, secondary, higher education / workplace).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-analytic evidence suggests socio-cognitive (Bandura/Zimmerman) interventions have higher impact in primary education (contain motivational/emotional aspects), whereas metacognitive-focused interventions show stronger effects for secondary students; higher education may benefit from motivational/emotional focus (self-efficacy, goal setting). Tailor theory choice and intervention components to student age and task demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive load and SRL skill development sequencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation to adopt a SRL skill developmental approach (observation, emulation, practice/automatization, self-regulation) that accounts for cognitive load and scaffolds learners over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zimmerman's Multi-Level model stages (observation, emulation, practice including automaticity, and self-regulation) are recommended. Instructional design should minimize extraneous cognitive load (per cognitive load theory) and progressively scaffold SRL skills so practice leads to automatization before expecting autonomous self-regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautions for SSRL / group-based interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence-based warning that group-based SRL interventions can have differential or even detrimental effects depending on educational level and implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dignath et al. found SSRL/group work detrimental for primary students but beneficial for secondary students. Implement SSRL interventions cautiously in younger learners and provide appropriate scaffolding and structure to maximize positive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement and technological scaffolding of SRL
rubrics_metrics.description: Guideline to use recent SRL measurement advances and computer-based scaffolding to better measure and support SRL processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review highlights new SRL measurement developments and the use of computers not only to measure but to scaffold SRL (e.g., MetaTutor). These tools allow more tailored interventions and fine-grained, longitudinal measurement (learning diaries, digital traces); integrate modern measurement methods when evaluating SRL.
